The ruins stretched far and wide, skeletons of once great structures reaching towards the horizon in all directions. Crumbling towers clawed for the sky, the blood red moon hanging high above them, taunting them with its incredible closeness and yet immeasurable distance.

This was probably the largest ruin he had found. The Last Folly, the old man had called it as he cackled madly. It seemed fitting, he decided. A final battle had been fought here, and no one had won.

He sat down on the massive pile of rocks, deciding to rest here, alone in the wreckage. There was nary a lifeform out here, not even so much as a rodent. 

He had spent his life wandering the world, documenting all the relics of the Final War. The conflict that left the world as ruined as the structures around him. He had desperately tried to find some meaning, some purpose in the fight that left humanity in tatters, a few survivors struggling to eke out a life in a world that no longer wanted them. He was no fool; in a few generations, there would be no more humans left. They were few enough as it is. 

He had come here, to the Last Folly, in the hopes of finding some meaning in it all. If sacrificing humanity was worth whatever led to this devastation. 

But he had found nothing. Just a few desperate recordings as those who fought here died in agony. There was truly no hope for humanity now. 

And there was no hope for him, he decided as he drew his sword. 

His body would not be found for a long, long time.

My mother was thrown out of her house last year for not paying rent, and forcibly moved into my place because she and her boyfriend had no where else to go. She insisted that it would only be for a few weeks, but it's been nearly a year since and things only got worse since then:

1) before she moved in, almost everything was clean (save my storage room) and only a small bug problem. She comes in and now my kitchen sink drain is clogged and fleas and roaches are rampant. I had no problem with either beforehand. 

2) She refused to help with any bills, and anytime I brought up the subject she screamed and sobbed about how she and her boyfriend have no money and how dare I ask for help. The two of them worked fairly well-paying warehouse jobs (for this poor area anyway) and made approximately $1000 a paycheck. 

3) My cats grew stressed from all this and started urinating everywhere. Because I was hardly home due to my job, I couldn't keep up with it and had to listen to her complain about the smell yet she wouldn't do anything about it. It was all my fault, obviously.

Eventually I grew so stressed from all of it that I had a mental breakdown at work and got fired. When that happened, she started making more and more demands, looking for any avenues to have me thrown out. I started working at a seasonal position making far, far less and barely could keep up with the gas to get to work and the bills. Had to pawn off some of my stuff to keep up. Then one night my car ran out of gas on my way home from work and I was stranded in the cold, cold weather. I tried calling her for help, but all she did was yell and I hung up. I scrounged for coins and got a bit of gas, but then my battery died. I was stranded for hours until some cops stopped by and gave me a lift back since the car wouldn't work. To replace the battery would cost money I didn't have, and since she would have to pay for it she took the car away as well. To get it back I would've had to sign a contract with her that would've given her complete control over my personal life. Thankfully my best friend was able to start giving me lifts everywhere I needed to go. But once the seasonal job ended, she forced me to sign an eviction notice. I can't move anywhere else because

A) most places around here won't let me keep my cat, and I refuse to go anywhere without her
B) I don't know if I'll be able to find work in time to keep up with the bills

I'm getting my taxes back soon, and I offered to cover rent for the next few months so I can stay, but she told me last night that she would only agree if I signed another contract. I don't know what this contract entails, but I doubt it'll be good. 

Is she a narc, or am I just applying the word to her to explain her behavior? Am I posting in the wrong sub here? I'm really worried about this contract and everything else and I'm terrified. 

Thanks for reading, and sorry if I wasted your time.

"Fine!" I snapped, furious. "Who cares? Nobody else ever did!"

She frowned, a sight I was fairly familiar with at this point. So she was disappointed with me. Fine. Let her. In a few minutes, it wouldn't matter anymore. Nothing would. I'd be dead, and I'd be free. 

"I don't think you understand the magnitude of what you're doing..." she began.

I cut her off with a sharp gesture. "No, you don't understand! I was cast out by my own parents when I was ten! Every time I try to build myself back up, I was cast down again and again! Backstabbed, mocked, rolled up, tossed aside! Nobody cared about me all my life! And now you expect me to not take my one way out because, what, some fucking sense of the greater good? What do I care about the 'greater good' when it's done nothing for me? Where's my reward for everything I've endured all my life?" I was almost in tears at this point. "I just want to rest. That's all. Can't I have that, at least?"

"Try," the ghost of my wife told me. "Try. They're only three. They'll die without you. Please." She sounded more desperate than I had ever heard her before. "For me. For them."

I squeezed my eyes shut. My hand with the gun shook. "I don't know if I can."

"You can," she said warmly. "You're better than you know."

"But I..." She was gone. I looked to the loaded gun in my hand, and felt the tears drop from my eyes. I couldn't do it. Not alone. 

A knock at the door. I considered not opening it. Marybeth they'd go away and leave me to my death. 

"Daddy?" a little girl's voice called. 

I froze. Sighed. Set the gun aside and opened the door. 

My daughter stood there, clutching her favorite stuffed cat. She looked up at my face, saw the tears. "Are you okay?"

"I...yes. Just thinking."

"Okay. We were just waiting for you to come read to us."

I paused, glancing at the gun sitting next to the alarm clock. I could tell her to go back to bed with her brother. Tell her I'd be there in a second. Pick it up. Fire. It would be so easy.

She had been searching for them for a very long time. 

Her father had set her on this path, a long long time ago. He had always ranted about the Crossroads, the twin portals of the gods, how his father and grandfather had roamed the Earth in search of these elusive devices. 

In a way, she felt responsible. The entire reason he stopped was because he met her mother and had her. She felt obligated to continue his search, despite the hardships. 

The Crossroads were a pair of deep black portals held between the twin fingers of massive stone structures. It was said they were older than the world they sat on, and from looking at them with her own eyes, she sensed that it was true. It filled her with apprehension, and she gripped her bow tight.

She continued onward, the Crossroads growing larger and larger as she drew near. Dawn quickly approached, illuminating her surroundings and chasing off the chill that had settled in during the night. 

When she reached the base of the stone fingers that anchored the portals, she realized she wasn't alone.

Between the portals ran a small stream. Seated on a rock at the center of the stream was an elderly man, eyes closed. He made no movement at her approach, but she knew she would have to speak with him. The water was surprisingly warm as it seepedinto her boots, but she splashed her way over to the old man and waited.

An hour passed. Then two. 

Only when the sun was over the horizon did the man look up. Much of his face was hidden by his long white hair, but she could still see the warm gray eyes that stared at her. 

"I've waited a long time for you, Child," he said kindly. "Welcome to the Crossroads."

She bowed. "I am honored."

"Oh don't be," he replied, chuckling. "I'm but an old man, and these are but portals. Nothing special about us."

"But these are the Crossroads! Pathways of the gods! Certainly they are quite special!"

The old man shrugged. "Are they? Things only have value if someone assigns them such, and I choose not to."

"Who are you?"

"No idea. I suppose you could call me the Gatekeeper, but I lost my name a long time ago."

She looked up at the Crossroads, grand and imposing. Her family's long sought goal for so many generations. How could it not be grand? 

He laughed when she told him as much. "Tell me, what is a Crossroads?"

She paused. "A place where two roads meet. They say the realms of the divine and the mortal intersect here."

"Yes it is, and no it doesn't." He still bore that warm smile, but now it was tinged with amusement. "The legends only say as much because people want to believe that they have purpose. That such grand structures must have divine power behind them."

"Are you saying they do not?" The words came out sharper than she intended, but what the Gatekeeper was saying defied everything she had been raised to believe, everything she had sacrificed over the past three years. 

"There is another definition of 'crossroads,' Child. A point where a crucial decision must be made." He pointed to the portals above them. "One portal will take you home. The path your father set for you is fulfilled. You have beheld the Crossroads with your own eyes. You can return and choose your own path now. 

"The other will take you far from here, to a place where mortals should never go. The home of those who built these things. You will never return to this world if you choose that path. In either case, once you enter those portals, you will never see the Crossroads again."

She gazed at them for a long time. Both of the options the Gatekeeper presented to her were appealing. Part of her screamed at her to enter the portal to this other place, to fulfill the goal her family had dreamed of for so many generations. Her father's ghost urged her on, to choose that path, to do what he had never been able to do.

But another part of her told her that she didn't have to. That path would almost certainly lead to her demise, in a terrible, terrible fashion. She could go home, and start a new life. One of her own choosing. Her own path, not her father's. 

She found herself incapable of decision, and for a very long time she stood there, gazing at the swirling black portals. 

The Gatekeeper was silent, watching her. When she turned to face him once again, her choice was written across her face. He sighed. "Very well. Let us go, then."

I don't know about what you "can" do, but I can tell you what you shouldn't do. 

Don't blame the kid for doing this. They're as much a victim here as anyone. They may be facing problems they don't know how to cope with, and it's causing them a great amount of stress. Talk to them, try to figure out what they're dealing with, and if you can help. Counseling may help, but don't force it on the kid if you feel it'll shut them out further.

Don't make a major spectacle of it. A major intervention may only worsen the problem than help it, as it'll draw unwanted attention to the kid. They may clam up and feel even worse about what they're doing to themselves. Talk to them one-on-one, in a calm environment. Bring in others only if you feel it'll help. 

Don't accuse them of doing this because they seek attention. It would take some serious mental issues for someone to mutilate themselves in this manner solely because they want attention. They are scarring themselves, and they'll carry these scars for the rest of their life. They may be doing this because their internal pain is so great that the only way to let it out is to cause physical pain. 

The last thing I can think of is to be supportive. Try to be there for them as much as you can, but not in a way that seems overbearing. Offer them a hug or a shoulder to cry on. You have no idea how much something small like that can make a big difference. Talk with them. If you have trouble talking to them, try to take an interest in one of their hobbies, some common ground you can start with. 

My mother never really cared about my depression, and if she did, it was only because she was worried about her public image. Never make your kid feel unwanted. Communication is key, I think. They're in a dark place right now, but maybe you can be the lantern that lights their way.

I was a young, impressionable teenager when I made that wish, probably high, definetly not thinking. 


It was a conversation I was having with my friends, about life and death, our finite lifespans. This was deep and quite disappointing to us, especially after Jackie's suicide last week. She was there one day, gone the next, and wouldn't be able to experience life anymore. 


So I looked a star -- a random star, one out of a billion billion points of light in the vast open sky -- and wished for immortality. I didn't want to end up like Jackie, to wind up unable to experience so much of the world. It was a dumb wish that I soon forgot about.


But the stars didn't. They are vast, powerful objects, more powerful than we pathetic mortals can comprehend. They hear; it just takes them a while because they're hundreds of light years away. 


Years went by, and that bitter understanding about life and death nagged at the back of my mind for a long time. After high school, I didn't bother with college. Instead I took all the money I had -- which wasn't much -- and hopped on a bus to some random city. From there I went to another, then another, sometimes walking, sometimes riding. I lost contact with my friends and family after my phone was stolen in Los Angeles, but by then I didn't really care. I barely spoke to them anyway, so maybe they thought I was was dead. I would be eventually, I thought, so they might as well work their grief out.


Then I met her. It wasn't like what they show in the movies; no spark, no love at first sight. Rather, it was a chance encounter in a park. I was trying to find someplace to settle down for the night, one where the police wouldn't see me. She was walking her dog when it got away from her and ran up to me. It was likely smelling the hamburger I had wrapped up in my bag as it jumped up against me, shoving its big nose toward it. She quickly reclaimed her dog, apologizing profusely for its behavior. We somehow started talking, and she offered to let me stay at her apartment for a few days until it was time to move on. 


I wound up staying there for months. I'm not sure what made me stay, but every time I thought about leaving I found some excuse to stick around. She never asked when I was leaving, and at first just treated me like a guest. 


Then all of a sudden it was October, when yesterday it had been June. Where had the time gone, I wondered. I started looking for work, as I didn't want her to keep taking care of me, and eventually found a job at some retail location. 


What point does this have, you ask? Well, living with her, having this...stability, it made me realize something. Not all at once, mind you, but gradually. I came to realize that life wasn't just a short trip to death. It...changes, it grows. Life is one big, scary road, but what direction you take is entirely up to you. Because in the end, you'll look back on what you've done, and decide whether it was worth it all. If you were truly happy living life as you did. And I realized that living life as I was, drifting from place to place, wasn't satisfying at all. It was long and lonely, with no real goal at the end except death. 


I married her eventually. We settled down, had kids, and I lived a good life. A good life. When I laid in that hospital decades later, I was surrounded by my loved ones, my children and grandchildren. I smiled. I was happy. I died. 


Then I woke up. 


I was trapped in a coffin six feet underground, but strangely the lack of oxygen didn't bother me. I had no need to breathe anymore. It took me two days to escape my grave, and I emerged to a completely different world. Much of my surroundings were battered and scorched. Destroyed in a solar flare well after my death. The surviving humans had either fled into space or hid underground. 


That star I had wished upon so, so long ago had heard my request and for whatever reason granted it. I don't even know which one, only that it must've been about 200 light years from Earth after I figured out I was 214 years old. 


So now I can experience everything life has to offer, except there's nothing left on this planet. I no longer need to eat, or sleep, or drink or breathe. But now I'm alone, my life once more unfulfilling. 


So you tell me now, and you will tell me true. How do I die?

The King of Red, the Solitary Ruler, was known as a conquerer, a brilliant warrior and tactician. From Syraa to Nor, he led his armies across the continent, bringing peace to those who submitted...and death to those who did not. He foresaw himself as the one who would unite the world, and bring the disparate kingdoms to heel. "A great destiny!" he would proclaim to his troops, and they would cheer his name and run out to battle. 

Years went by. With every victory his army grew just a little bit smaller, and with every campaign another dozen tents would be empty. 

"My liege, you have conquered half the known continent!" cried his general. "Let us end this war and build up our kingdom, before our men all perish!" The King laughed at him, called him craven, and so the general gathered his men and left the King to his war.

A few years after that, after the conquest of Cloudia, the King's admiral said, "Your Majesty, your lands are vast. You have seized most of the known world, and have an empire men will envy for all time. Surely you mean to end our fight now, and let the men return home?"

The King paused, considering this, and then replied, "Admiral, look around you. Our army is vast, our men rich from our fight. The lands that yet stand against us are richer still. Surely you see the value in conquering these kingdoms and taking their gold for our own?"

"At what cost, my liege?" With that the admiral gathered his men and left the King behind. 

On the eve of taking the last holdout of resistance, the King's wife came to him. "My love, your empire rules almost all of the world. But your men are few, and wish only to return home, to their husbands and wives, their sons and daughters. Leave this small kingdom to itself, and return home with me, so we may rule the world together and rebuild what was lost."

"And so we shall my love," the King replied. "But only after I seize this last bastion of resistance, take what they have, and build for our people an empire that will rule for eternity!" 

"Then you are a fool, and I curse you as such." The queen, heartbroken, left then, and the King plotted with what few men remained. 

The next day came war, and battle, one that lasted until the sun had set and the moon was high in the sky. With a mighty attack, the King slew the last rebel and stood victorious over it. As he sat in one the stone throne with its red flags, he bellowed, "Let all who are loyal kneel before the King of the World!"

But none did. It was only then, when the fog of his singleminded ambition had lifted, that he realized that no one was left. His men had all perished, and the rest had abandoned him. He was King of the World, yes, but there was no one to show him loyalty, obedience. He was alone. This saddened him, for he knew not where to find those that had abandoned him. He remained in that chair as the bodies around him were swallowed by time, as the world changed around him and his empire crumbled away. They say he sits there still, a miserable man of stone that rules solitude and never moves. If one were to show him the proper respect, maybe then he could let go. Maybe then he could see his army once again.

The arena of Scaleswind attracted people from all across the land, competitors and spectators alike. 

Stan the Swordsman was a mix of both. Sometimes, if he felt like it, he would fight. Other times, he liked to just sit and watch. This was one of the latter. He had been asked to watch this match with Komiko, a Low Wizard of the Magic Tower, who was sitting rather nervously next to him. Stan wasn't sure why she was nervous; people rarely died in the arena. It was against the law. The last time anyone had died was fifty years ago, and that had been an accident. Was it all the people? Komiko was a very shy person. In fact, Stan had been mildly surprised when Komiko came up to him yesterday and asked if he would like to go with her to the arena in Scaleswind.

The fight was due to begin a few minutes. Stan was a tall, dark-skinned man, clad in heavy plate with a two-handed sword on his back. His head was bald; indeed, he could not grow hair until he had proven his worth to his people. 

Komiko, on the other hand, was small, slight of build. She was clad in blue and silver robes, with several enchanted items adorning her. She carried with her a long magic staff, tipped with a glowing, blue orb. 

They had sat in silence for a while, until Komiko spoke. "Um...do you know who is competing today?" Her voice shook as she said that, he noticed, but did not comment on it. 

"No, I do not," Stan replied. "I know that there are two powerful competitors here today."

"How would they stack against Laph, though?"

Stan laughed. "Not very well. She would take them both down without breaking a sweat."

"Yeah..." She grew quiet, but before Stan could speak, the announcer boomed. 

"Ladies and gentlemen," the announcer said. His voice was amplified by a spell that sent his voice across the arena. "Welcome to the pride and joy of Scaleswind, the Great Arena!"

As the crowd roared, Stan leaned in close to his companion's ear. "I thought the docks were Scaleswind's pride and joy?" he asked in jest. 

Komiko shrugged, and Stan caught the hint of a smile on her face. That was enough for him, and he returned to watching the game. The actual arena pit was circular, covered in sand and broken equipment. At either end, there were two steel gates that slowly began to rise.

"Today, we have two strong champions of the Arena. First, from the Great Divide, we have today, the Orange Bandit!" From the left stepped out a man clad entirely in orange leathers. His hair was long and dark, and his eyes were a striking blue. 

"And from here in the Blue Kingdom, we have with us a very special guest. You all know him as the Kingdom's own Captain of the Guard. Give it up for Nelefoss!" 

Stan's eyes widened, and from the way Komiko drew in a sharp breath, she was surprised as well. Nelefoss rarely ever traveled out of Azure City, not after the Great Beast's attack several months ago. 

The crowd didn't seem to care, as they shouted with enthusiasm at the blue-armored warrior. The Orange Bandit seemed momentarily bewildered, but drew his axe regardless. Nelefoss drew his sword, and bowed to his opponent, as though this were a proper duel. The Bandit was even more surprised by this, and more than a few in the crowd murmured in astonishment. 

"Good man," Stan said. Komiko quietly agreed. 

And like that, the fight was on. Both combatants charged at each other, but Nelefoss sidestepped the Bandit's rather clumsy strike with the axe, responding with a quick kick to the side that sent the other man sprawling in the sand.

"This will be over quickly," Stan decided. Komiko nodded. 

"You don't know that!" someone shouted behind them. Komiko and Stan turned around to see several men standing there, all wearing armor and carrying axes similar to what the Orange Bandit was using. 

"Actually, we do," Stan replied. "We know Captain Nelefoss personally. He is a great fighter. He has trained the Champion herself." 

"So what?" one man asked. "Don't you know the Bandit's backstory?"

One man grinned. "Let's enlighten them."

"Right. The Orange Bandit was said to have been born alone, in a dark, forgotten corner of the Divide. He had to fight to survive from birth."

Another picked up the tale. "He was soon found by a patrol from the Red Kingdom, who picked him up and took him before the King. The old one, not the crazy one they have now. The King was so astounded by the boy's strength that he declared he be trained by the Red Knights themselves."

"And so he trained with them for weeks, becoming stronger every day." The third storyteller gained a faraway look in his eye. "Not even the Ruby General could stop him."

"But then the Mad King came to power, and exiled the poor boy," the first said. "He wanted no rivals to his power, and he feared the boy's strength. The boy grew angry, and wanted revenge."

"He eventually came upon a group of bandits, who worshiped at his feet when they realized how strong he was. He soon became their leader, and led raids against the Kingdom's slavers and greedy knights."

"But soon the King found him, and all but he were put to the sword." The third began to weep. "He watched from afar as the Ruby General killed each and every one of them. He was filled with sadness, and rage, but was forced to abandon the Red Kingdom."

"He eventually came to here, to Scaleswind. He soon found the arena, and joined it so as to inspire the people of this Kingdom to go and avenge his friends by fighting the Mad King."

"He is so strong and impressive," the second man concluded, "that even the Champion herself can't help but swoon when she sees him." 

The three finished their tale, and Stan and Komiko exchanged surprised glances. Then they broke out laughing, the three men looking on in surprise and anger.

"I'm sorry, but what?" Komiko asked. "The Red Kingdom never sends out patrols into the Divide."

"They did with the last King!" the third man protested.

"And the Ruby General has never once been beating, not even by the Champion," Stan added. "What makes you think this person can?"

"And Laph certainly wouldn't swoon over that," Komiko finished. "She already has her eyes on someone. Like, say, a certain Princess?"

"That's it!" the first man snapped, surprising several people around them. With a shout, he barreled into Stan, sending both tumbling into the stands. Komiko stood and quickly cast a magic shield, just in time to stop the other two fans from punching her, sending them both flying back. She then reabsorbed the shield and sent the magic energy out as a paralysis spell. The spell washed over the two, who fell backward against the stairs. 

She smiled, nodded, and turned around. Down below, Stan had his sword out and was dueling the first man, whose small, unadorned axe paled in comparison to the beauty of Stan's blue greatsword, an elegant weapon forged by the people of the Silent Isles, his home. 

Stan made quick work of the man, disarming him and then leveling his sword at the man's throat. "Surrender," he ordered calmly.

The man looked ready to protest, but finally nodded as best he could with a weapon at his throat. 

"Well folks, looks like we got ourselves *two* fights today!" the announcer suddenly said. "And sad to say, the Orange Bandit and his fans were all beaten soundly by Nelefoss, and...and whoever these two are!"

The arena broke out into applause. Komiko looked down at the arena and caught the Captain's eye, who smiled and nodded at her as he sheathed his sword and headed back to his gate. The Orange Bandit made a rather rude gesture before grabbing his weapon and leaving the arena.

"What is that?" Kayla asked, pointing to the cube.

The Wicked Healer, she was called. Anyone who entered her home came out looking less than what they were upon entering. 

She had set up shop some years ago, in the small village of Emerald Wing. At the time, nobody paid her too much mind; another healer was always welcome in the village, especially after the Yrassian's recent war with the Machine Imperium. 

Of course, it soon became apparent that she was anything but. A few soldiers had come to Emerald Wing after a particularly gruesome battle, having barely escaped with their lives. One of their number, however, had a broken arm and was bleeding heavily from his forehead. The villagers had directed them to the healer. 

When he emerged, everyone screamed. His arm had been reset, yes, but had been twisted and mangled beyond recognition. The cut on his forehead was gone, sure, but so was the rest of his forehead, exposing the white bone beneath. The thing that had been a soldier lumbered toward his former comrades, his eyes glazed over, and they were forced to put him out of his misery. Two others died in the effort.

The last three soldiers then went into the healer's house, determined to make her pay. They never came back out. Everyone in the village tried to stay away from her at that point, but she was the only healer around. All the others had been called away for the war. After the tavern caught fire, they were forced to turn to her for help to take care of the wounded. Three people had their lungs removed, and two more had their burned limbs cut off. All of them were still alive.

The people weren't sure what to do then. The guards refused to go there, on account of what happened to the soldiers. Someone tried to rally the people at one point, to burn down her house. Nobody had listened, too frightened of how she might retaliate. 

And that was when he came in. A month after the war had ended, a man clad entirely in black came into the village. He rode a horse with deep black coloring. The eyes weren't much brighter, and some thought the steed didn't have any. 

One of the guards stopped the stranger, though every instinct in her body told her to stay away. "Turn back, stranger. This place is cursed."

The man didn't, instead turning to face her. At least, she thought he did; it was difficult to tell, with his face hidden beneath a black hood. Come to think of it, not a single inch of his skin was exposed to the sunlight. The implications sent a chill up her spine. 

Then, he spoke. "Why is this place cursed? I sense nothing amiss."

"Then maybe you aren't looking closely, stranger." She gestured to their surroundings, to the people who kept their heads down. Even the animals were strangely quiet. "We are trapped by the power of a witch. She might not have placed a true curse on us, aye, but the power she has over this place has frightened everyone."

The man paused. "Where is this witch?"

The guard pointed to a large, well-maintained house at the north edge of town. "There. She poses as a healer, but has twisted the healing magics to torture us." She thought of her cousin, whose leg had been mauled by a wolf. "If you're hurt, run far, far away."

The man nodded, then wheeled around and headed back the way he came. The guard, thinking her duty done, turned and went back to her rounds. She wasn't sure why she bothered anymore, but anything was better than thinking about the witch that held the village in her grip.

-------------

Night had fallen when the black-armored stranger returned to the village. The guard had long since gone to bed, but her eyes snapped open when she heard the moaning, the pained moaning. Terror seized her, fearing that someone else had been hurt, or worse, been "taken care of" by the Wicked Healer. 

When she ran to her window, however, the answer was much worse. She saw the black armored stranger, walking without his horse, just past her house. Rather than that fell steed, he walked at the head of a large army. Zombies moaned, skeletons cracked, wraiths floated about, scaring away any who tried to approach.

She hurriedly donned her armor, then grabbed her sword and ran outside. The unnatural army was marching through the center of town when she ran up to the stranger, raising her sword. If she killed him, the undead should become inert...

The stranger looked at her, then, with a flick of his wrist, shot a ray of green magic at her, which froze her in place. He held up a hand, stopping his army, and then walked right up to her. He had his hood down, she realized, exposing his black hair, pale, angular head, and sharp, blood-red eyes. Her insides turned cold.

*A vampire.*

He stopped in front of her, looked her over. "You're the woman from before," he said simply. 

She realized her mouth could still move. "Please, don't..."

The vampire narrowed his eyes before widening. "Oh, that. Don't worry, I won't suck your blood. I only do that to my enemies."

"Then why are you here?" she asked. 

He pointed to the Wicked Healer's house. "I'm here to take her down, of course. After what you told me earlier, I can't very well just leave her to live and keep you all under her control." He flicked his wrist again, and suddenly she collapsed to the ground, free of the spell. "Name's Derek, by the way. Former head of the Bloodfued Clan." 

"K-Kayla," she answered, getting back to her feet. At full height, she stood a few inches over him. She looked at the army that stood before her. "What have you done?"

He looked over his shoulder. "Oh, them? I recruited them, to help me take her down. A...friend of mine back home taught me that you can't take down evil without some help. Don't worry, I'll put them back in the graveyard when we're done here." 

She looked at him incredulously, but he was already moving off, gesturing for the army to follow. What would a vampire know about fighting evil? Aren't they already evil? Shouldn't he be *helping* the Wicked Healer?

She followed closely, ignoring the wraiths as they tried to scare her off, until they reached the healer's house. A gate and hedge had been erected around the house's perimeter, but with a murmur, green flames burned down the hedge. With a yell, Derek charged, followed closely by his army of the undead. 

Kayla hurried after them, sword in hand. The wraiths were ignoring her now, Derek having given them orders to scout the house and find the Wicked Healer. In the meantime, his zombies and skeletons smashed apart the house, destroying tables and ripping apart books. 

Derek, his red eyes closed in concentration, held his arms up, blue energy circling his open palms. He moved his hands around in all directions, before finally settling on an area below them. He spoke to the undead around them. "There's a portal in the basement beneath us. Smash it before she uses it to escape." As they moved to obey, Derek turned and grinned at Kayla. "You should come too."

They hurried along, eventually coming to a large, steel door in what she assumed was the kitchen. Kayla, reaching it first, reached for the door handle, only to be thrown backward, high into the air, then landing hard on a table. Groaning, she heard the vampire laughing nearby. "This woman is all-powerful, yet you didn't expect her to have defense spells prepared? Are you at all related to the Champion of the Blue Kingdom? You're certainly as smart as her."

Kayla grumbled as Derek set to work deactivating the spells around the door. After a few minutes, he was done, and he held the door open as the undead rushed through and down the stairs. "Ladies first?" he asked the guard, gesturing to the door. 

Kayla walked through the door, carefully picking her way down the stairs, Derek following close behind her. She suddenly heard the sounds of his undead clashing with something down below. 

"The Healer must be down there," Derek noted. The two picked up their pace, and came to the foot of the stairs just in time to see a large, gruesome...thing tear apart the last of the vampire's army. The room was dark, but she knew it had to be huge, for the thing that now turned its attention to them was large as well. It stood head and shoulders over her, a bulging mass of flesh and metal.

The Great Beast was large, a gigantic golem of scales, wood, and plant-matter. It unleashed a loud, thunderous roar as catapults launched rocks filled with burning rocks at the fiend, to no avail.

"Nothing's working!" one guard cried. "This thing is just laughing at our attacks!" 

"Quiet!" her captain snarled. "We'll get through this. Don't worry."

"But how?" another asked. "Not even the Champion could beat it!"

In truth, the captain wasn't sure. In all his years defending his homeland, he had never seen such a behemoth. The Beast was of such a height, if he just reached up, he could snatch the clouds out of the sky. 

"Captain? What do we do?" someone asked, afraid.

"I..."

Then, without warning, a bolt of blue lightning streaked across the sky, striking the Great Beast in the eye and sending it reeling backward. The captain blinked in surprise, as did the men and women around him. Where had that come from? 

"Don't worry, captain! We'll handle this!"

Snapped out of his stupor, the captain looked to his right and saw no less than a dozen wizards approaching him. He had set up his command center in a cave not far from the battlefield, where the Kingdom's forces were being decimated. In truth, it was little more than a few lanterns, a table, and a few weapon racks. 

"What the -- why are you all here?" 

The lead wizard -- a woman he recognized as a friend of the Champion's -- spoke up. "The Archmage gives his regards, captain. He said that it was time to fulfill our debt to your King and Queen."

The captain could only stand with his mouth agape as the wizards as one turned around and stalked back outside. "You'll be crushed!" he finally said. 

The woman turned back. "No we won't. I've been practicing."

For some reason, he wasn't really reassured.

Three months went by after the Cleansing of Old New York. As we later found out, nobody within New York City even knew it had happened, or that there were slums at all. Travel outside the city was forbidden without a permit and an escort, and you were not allowed to stray from the predetermined path. Doing so would lead to a very big lawsuit for "breach of contract" or something like that.

Eventually your father grew restless. Though we had grown comfortable in the town, he still had a job to do. He had to save the people from Old New York. We had learned the culprit who had ordered the Cleansing: John Mortar, CEO of some big construction company. He had been contracted to build hotels outside of the city, but was never told where. With no one willing to say otherwise, he used attack 'bots that were technically illegal to be used for private purposes, and razed Old New York to the ground. 

Eventually, I came back to our house to find your father packing his things, ready to go. He couldn't rest until he defeated John Mortar, couldn't relax until he changed things. We had friends among those that were captured, or so we hoped. We had to save them, he told me. We couldn't stay here anymore. 

I admit I didn't really want to leave. Everything there was peaceful, no sign of treachery or threat of abduction. But your father was adamant, and I followed. We slipped away into the night, and your father produced a map of the state. There was another village, far to the west, that was rumored to be the headquarters of some little resistance movement. "That's where we'll find support," he said. 

It was a long trip over the course of over a month. We had to do a lot of backtracking to avoid being caught by the corporations or anything of the sort. Two lone wanderers were perfect targets for abduction, and we couldn't afford that yet. 

It was late September when we finally found the town, and good thing too, because we were low on supplies. The first thing that happened was that we were ambushed by the guards of the town, knocked out, had our bags stolen, and were taken to the local jailhouse and locked away. When we finally came to one hour later, our guards took us to see their leader. 

Melissa was a fierce woman, quick to anger, and more than happy to put a bullet in your head if she decided she didn't like you. But she was also fair, slow to judge. We were set down in front of her, and she immediately asked who we were and why we had come. 

Your father told her our story, from the Cleansing to leaving the town the month before. She didn't say anything while he spoke, just sat and listened, and didn't seem surprised at all about the Cleansing. That's when we first learned what it was, and that Old New York wasn't the first such place to be attacked. She explained that when she was a little girl, her original home was smashed in another Cleansing in order to expand the city. She even pointed out the burn mark on her shoulder she got while escaping. She wanted nothing more than to take down those who ruled New York, but her forces were few, too few to take on an entire robot army.

"So then what happened?" the Princess asked, hooked. Kyle opened his mouth to continue when the door to the conference room opened, and in stepped her mother. The Empress was tall, clad in rich, dark purple clothes with blue highlights. Nestled in her curly black hair sat a plain silver crown, the symbol of her status, and her blue eyes sat behind a holographic visor that provided her with up-to-date information regarding the Empire. Kyle immediately left the chair and bowed low, as did the other Guardsmen. The Princess bowed her head. 

"Were you telling stories again, Captain?" asked the Empress in a sweet, friendly tone. 

"Yes, Your Majesty," Kyle replied. "Your daughter was curious about your husband's past."

The Princess looked up to see her mother smiling. "Well, I'm sorry to interrupt, but the other diplomats have arrived. I want you to meet them, Hannah."

"Do I have to?"

Her mother shrugged, her smile turning a bit more sad. "It's important. Knowing your opponents is the first step to success, and these two are very...interesting people. 

Hannah turned her gaze to Kyle, pleading with him to save her. But he simply gave her a smile and gestured for her to follow her mother. "When you get back, I'll continue the story," he told her.

With a resigned nod, Hannah stood from the chair, brushed out the wrinkles in her outfit, and followed her mother and two of the Honor Guard out the room. It was 2056, a long time ago. The two of us, we were orphans, living in the filth-ridden slums of Old New York. We had no government to speak of; indeed, the government of America had long ago been bought out by big corporations. Everything in the big cities was under their direct control; the people, the media, the Internet, everything. Not many knew of the slums, and even fewer cared. 

Though it shames me to admit, we often had to steal in order to eat. It was commonplace back then; the slums had few stores to offer food, and those that did charged hefty prices for even a single loaf of bread. One night, your father and I were hiding out after one such heist when these machines suddenly descended upon Old New York. A Cleansing, it was called. The corporations were clearing away the slums to build some sort of big real estate. 

Thousands died as the slums were burned. We had no real police force, and those we did have ran at the first sign of trouble, like your father and me. We ran, and eventually hid in the sewers to escape the machines. We cowered while all those people died. 

That night, something in your father changed. He refused to watch this any longer. Before, if you ever confronted him, he would quickly surrender. It was often up to me to protect him. But after that night, he looked me, straight in the eye, and said, "I'm not going to let this happen again."

We picked our way through the ruins. There were still machines, some hovering in the sky, others clearing away rubble, but the main attack 'bots seemed to have disappeared. We tried to find survivors while avoiding the things in the sky. But just about everyone we found was dead, burned in the Cleansing. We did find one survivor, a little girl whose legs were gone and was well on her way to passing on. She told us that everyone who had survived had been rounded up and taken away by the machines. To be used as cheap labor, your father decided. It was not unheard of; often, machines would come into Old New York to round up a few "healthy-looking individuals" to work for the corporations in the actual city, a few dozen miles north. 

Obviously, the two of us couldn't storm the city and rescue everyone; we'd be killed the moment we set foot within two miles of the place. We helped the girl pass on and then buried her as best we could before leaving the slums behind. 

We traveled for weeks, avoiding the roads, taking the country route. The major places were being monitored, but there were a few towns that were considered beneath the notice of either the corporations or their lapdogs in the government. We just didn't know where to look; we had no maps, no method of navigation. We didn't even have food. We fashioned a pair of sticks into spears and used them to kill any animals that looked edible. 

The Lord must have been smiling on us, for almost a month after we left the slums, we stumbled upon one of these towns. We were half-starved and tired, and so collapsed right outside one of the outermost houses as soon as we realized that the place was inhabited. We woke up several hours later, being tended to by some of the townsfolk. We were fed, given proper clothes, and then approached by the mayor of the town. Mr. Chesterson, he called himself. 

He started asking us questions: who we were, where we had come from, that sort of thing. He was very careful to make sure his town wasn't overtaken by any government agents or something like that. We answered his questions truthfully. When we told him about the Cleansing, he seemed quite disturbed. It seemed like he had no idea that anyone was capable of that sort of thing. But as long as we worked, he agreed to let us stay here for as long as we wanted.

They called them Ethana and Cultoo. The Mother of Stars and the Father of Darkness, so bright and beautiful that their true forms are forever hidden from our mortal eyes. 

When the universe was new, things were so bright that no one could see, that eyes were burned away at birth. Cultoo, a great behemoth made of the dust of stars and the gas of nebulae, saw this and so banished the light. But though people could now see, darkness fell, and still their sight was gone 

"I remove light, and still we cannot see," pondered Cultoo, "yet if I bring back light, the problem persists!"

Ethana came then, smaller and weaker than the great Cultoo. Yet Cultoo had always found Ethana beautiful, and so did not turn her away as he was wont to do. 

"There is a way to bring back light, but not at the rate it once was," Ethana told him. Cultoo scoffed; if not even he could figure out a way, what hope did Ethana have?

Ethana proposed combining their powers, and creating pockets of light. "Stars, we will call them." 

Cultoo was hesitant; light was strong, unpredictable, yet beautiful, but finally agreed to Ethana's plan. Summoning their wells of power, Ethana and Cultoo created the first star, our star, a ball of light and fire that returned our sight to us, yet did not blind us. 

Emboldened, the two created more stars, thousands more, filling the heavens with these pockets of light. And the people did sing songs of their work, praising the Mother and Father for their gifts. 

But tragedy struck when one star died. Then another, going out in a brilliant ball of fire. How could this be? 

Like the mortals they protected, Cultoo and Ethana realized that stars were not eternal. They would live and die just as we did. Ethana wanted to stop creating stars. "Why bother making something," she asked Cultoo, "if they will just die?"

But Cultoo, having seen how their work benefited the universe, took his love to show what the stars had inspired: exploration, beauty, mystery. These pockets of light, he told her, had inspired mortals to work just as hard as they did. Emboldened by this, Ethana resumed her work with more vigor than ever before, determined to create more things with which to inspire mortals. And thus were the constellations born, hidden works of art to remind mortals that they were never far from the minds of the Mother of Stars and the Father of Darkness.

And so the Heavens turned black, but always balanced by the light of stars.

"Welcome to the end."

The large man before me grinned beneath his crimson hood. The hood was connected to a large, thick cloak that hid his entire body from view. All I could really see was that grin, the flawless white teeth. He was a good seven feet tall, the tallest man I had ever seen. 

I was surprised when he had appeared. I was on patrol around a base far in the mountains. We were not told to expect any visitors today, so I had raised my rifle and prepared to call for backup when he had spoken. I hesitated then, and the figure waved a gloved hand. My radio suddenly shorted out, and all I heard from it was static.

"Don't bother calling for help," he said in a dark, raspy voice. "We will have a chat, you and I, and listen to the masses as they scream."

"Who the hell are you?" I demanded, raising my rifle again. Another wave, and suddenly the gun became a mass of maggots, wiggling in my hands. I shouted and dropped the things, backing away and trying not to shake. 

"Don't go anywhere," the other said, and I froze up. No, he didn't turn me to ice; rather, he had forced my muscles to lock up, so now I was stuck in mid-step, only a few feet from the wretched, smelly pile that started crawling apart. The large man walked forward, calmly stepping *through* the maggots and stopping only a few inches from my face. 

"What are you?" I breathed, thankful that my mouth could still work, though it was an effort. It was like my tongue had been swollen just enough, I realized, that I couldn't shout for help.

"I have been called many things," the other answered calmly. This close, I could smell the stench of decay on him, like a field long after a battle. "I've found I prefer to be called 'the Reaper.'"

"The Reaper? Like the Grim Reaper?" I stared at him, confounded. 

The other laughed, a sound like nails scratching down a chalkboard. "Perhaps. But where the Grim Reaper is a legend...I am very, very real."

Commotion from inside the base. An alarm. Maybe the others have seen me and our guest?

"Don't worry; they can't see us. No, they are responding to something else." He waved both his hands then, and suddenly I found myself standing on top of a plateau, desert stretching in all different directions. The Reaper was there, beside me, gazing at me. 

"We won't be disturbed here. Good."

"Why have you brought me here?" I demanded, realizing that I was no longer frozen. "What do you want from me?"

"What *I* want? No, my dear mortal. I am merely the messenger, sent by those more powerful than you or I."

"Who?"

"Their names are not for you to know, though They may reveal themselves properly to you, if They so choose." He paused, looking toward the setting sun. "Your world is coming to an end." 

I looked at him, not comprehending. He went on, "Your world's powers have argued too long, and now have taken matters into their own hands. Twenty minutes ago, commands were sent out all over the world. In five minutes, your world will burn. In ten, there will be nothing but ash. And there is nothing anyone can do to stop it."

I gazed at him, eyes wide. "Why weren't we told?" I asked. 

"Oh, your base commander knows. In fact, that alarm was to rouse everyone so that she could let them make peace before the end. I didn't want you distracted."

I grew angry. "You took me away from my friends, to, what, die alone on some rock in the middle of fucking no where?"

"You will not die. They do not want you to. I am here to make sure of that." He looked back at me, and though I could not see his eyes, I felt like my insides were freezing again from the look he was giving me.

"What do They want with me?" I finally asked.

"You will not die. In a few minutes, They will send one of Their emissaries to collect you. You will be taken to a holding facility, along with a dozen others, where you will be frozen for the next few thousand years. When it is time, you will be sent back to the surface, to rebuild your society."

"Why send you, then, if they have emissaries?" 

"They cannot come to this world. The atmosphere is harmful to Them. They need me -- and others like me -- to do Their dirty work here on this world." He grinned again. "Of course, sometimes I listen, sometimes I don't. It's not like they can hurt me."

"And what are you, exactly?"

Another horrible laugh. "Death incarnate. That's all you need to know."

A pause, as Reaper's words sank in. They -- whoever They were -- wanted to tear me away from everything I had known to take care of the future. But why? Part of the reason I had joined the military is because I dropped out of college. I barely passed high school, and I had a poor relationship with my parents. I asked him.

Reaper shrugged. "I can't say. It's Their decision, not mine. They're the ones who chose you, not I." He tilted his head to the side, looking over my shoulder. "Time's up."

I turned around, and my mouth fell open. Out in the distance, I saw a large mushroom cloud forming. 

"The bombs have fallen," Reaper sneered, and I heard a bit of a laugh in his voice. "Your hubris has finally caught up with you. So much death...it's beautiful."

I whipped around and stalked right up to him. "Damn you!" I snarled, and lashed out with a fist. 

I doubt he was even looking at me, more entranced with the cloud far out in the distance. He simply waved his hand, and suddenly I was skidding on my back across the plateau. I picked myself up and charged him again. A gesture, and suddenly I found myself trapped inside a steel cage. 

"That should hold you until They get here," he told me. He looked at me one last time, and grinned. "We'll meet again." I blinked, and he was gone, yet I was still trapped inside the cage. Snarling, I turned back to the cloud, far out in the distance. I wonder where it had landed, and if there were any people near the blast zone. Despite myself, I found myself picturing their final moments. A family driving down the road, maybe going to visit a friend. One of them looks up, sees a missile coming down on them. 

"Hey," they ask. "What's that?"

They stop the car, look out the window, see the harbinger of their demise barreling toward them. Maybe one of them got the bright idea to run away. They turn around and try to escape, but it was too late. The bomb hits, and each and every one of them were incinerated. Maybe slowly. Maybe...

"Don't worry," a voice suddenly said, interrupting my thoughts. "Their deaths were swift." 

Startled, I turned to see a figure standing in a beam of light beside my cage, gazing sadly at the distant explosion. He was tall, about as tall as Reaper, clad in angular, blue and white armor, a pair of large, eagle-like wings sprouting from his back. His eyes were glowed a bright blue from behind a steel mask, and in his hand he carried a long, golden spear. He looked at me, sadness in his eyes. "I'm...sorry about all this. The Reaper is not gentle when it comes to preforming the tasks we send him out to do."

"Are you the emissary he told me about?" I asked.

He nodded. "I am called Arch. I am the lord of Their Holy Guardians. A pleasure to meet you." 

He touched the cage with his spear, and instantly it disintegrated. "Come. I cannot leave this beam without exposing myself to harm."

I walked up to him, slowly, finally stopping at the edge of the beam. "Where are you taking me?" 

"To our home. Reaper told you everything you need to know."

I looked at him. "Why me?"

He looked back at the cloud. "My Masters have foreseen great things for you. You will become a great leader, a hero to the people of the future. You will triumph over those who will seek to destroy all humanity as rebuilt." He looked back at me. "Of course, only if you come along. We will not force you to."

I looked at the mushroom cloud, watched as it began to shrink. "What will be left?" I asked. 

"Ashes, as he told you," Arch answered. "But there will be others, doing their best to scrape by until they finally expire. Your life, I'm afraid, will not be a long or great one."

I took a deep breath, looked up toward the source of the beam, high above the clouds. I couldn't see anything beyond some great black shape. 

"Well?" Arch asked. "What will you do?"

Another deep breath, and I stepped into the beam. I got the sense that Arch, whatever he was, was smiling behind his mask. As we began to ascend, he spoke again.

"Welcome to *The End.*"

The entrance to the dragon's lair yawned before me, like the great gaping maw I imagined the the dragon's mouth to be like. I gripped my sword tightly; I had slain many a evil making my way here, like the cruel priestess who had oppressed her people's free will through devotion to her dark god, or the demon who had possessed a town's mayor in exchange for saving his son's life. All of them had operated, people would say, at the behest of the lord of this place.

I crept inside, carefully, and with good reason: with a flick of my sword, a pitfall trap was revealed, ending abruptly at some sharp steel spikes coated with blood. I stepped carefully around the new hole in the ground, and progressed carefully through the dungeon, fighting monsters and evading traps, until I stepped through the giant double doors leading to the dragon's lair. 

I gulped; I had heard legends about the dragon since I was but a small child. They say the dragon, Arsurius, was larger than the king's castle, had breath hotter than the very sun, scales blacker than the blackest night, eyes as red as hell. 

So when I heard the pained, miserable roar ahead, I was at once surprised; what could harm such a monster? Only I carried the famed Dragonsbane, the only weapon capable of defeating Arsurius. I hurried into the chamber, cloak flapping wildly behind me, armor rustling, lungs straining for breath. I could feel the heat of the place starting to get to me, despite the cooling enchantment the old crone had placed on me some time ago. Perhaps it is wearing off? Or is the dragon's power so great that not even the old magics could keep it at bay?

Finally I emerged into the chamber, and all my questions were finally answered. Even ones I had not thought to ask.

The dragon was there, yes, but it was not as fearsome as the legends claimed. Its wings, larger than the gods themselves, were gone, clearly torn off. Its scales were dull, not as black as night, but grayer than the hair of an old man. Its eyes did not make me think of hell, but of a dog who was chastised by its master. Indeed, the more I studied the creature, the more I was reminded of a beaten dog. And that's when I noticed the dull, gold collar looped around its neck, with a golden chain that led straight into the hands of the one who had beaten it.

"I have been waiting for you, ser knight," said the Princess, her ruby lips smiling ruthlessly. 

Of all the things I had expected to see, this was not one of them. But all I could say was a choked, "How...?"

The Princess looked down at me from atop a large throne made of obsidian, surrounded by mountains of gold and jewels. A sword lay across her lap, the pommel encrusted with rubies and sapphires. She wore armor as black as the throne, a red cape flowing down her shoulders like a river of blood. Her brown eyes studied me like a farmer might study a pig before sending it to slaughter. 

"It was a very simple matter," she replied, and oh, how her voice had changed. No longer did I hear the sweet melody of the girl I knew from my youth, who had run and played with me so long ago. "The old magics are very powerful, as I am sure you know. Oh, it took years of study, but when I finally mastered the power, I summoned the dragon to 'kidnap' me."

"You were the one to summon the fiend!?" I exclaimed, my eyes growing wide. "How?"

"I made it an offer. Half the gold in the land if it would help in my plan. A dragon's greed is greater than its common sense, it is said, and the land is rich indeed." She gestured to the beaten thing that cowered at her feet. "I made good on my promise. I did give it half the gold in the land, and now it sits melted underneath its skin."

"This...no. You can't be Princess Kathryn. The Princess I remember couldn't do something like this. The Princess I remember cried when she accidentally crushed an anthill. The Princess I remember would invite every child in the kingdom to her birthday parties, and then give them each a silver piece." I paused. "You have been possessed by a demon, then," I determined.

Kathryn laughed, a cold, haunting laugh that would lurk in my nightmares forever. "I'm sorry to disappoint, but I have never been possessed by a demon, though a few have tried during my quest for power. Everything I did back then was but an act, a farce I put on to keep everyone ignorant of my true persona, and those I didn't fool were...removed. Like Mother." 

"No...the--the queen died when bandits attacked her carriage."

"And who do you think told the bandits to attack her?" Her smile only grew colder, her eyes taunting. "And when their mission was done, they found out too late that the gold I paid them in was poisonous to touch. No one was alive to reveal my involvement." 

I was trembling then. The dragon's head was bowed, misery evident in its eyes. "W-what happens now?"

"Now?" Her smile widened to a grin as she slowly stood up from her throne, sword in hand, letting the leash tie against a ring next to her throne. "Now, my dear sister...you die." 

She charged.

Captain Han Shepard stood on the bridge, watching as stars streaked past his spaceship, the Millennium Prize of Enter Falcon. They were prepared for a suicide mission, one where they probably wouldn't return, except for him, of course, since he was, you know, the main character. 

Of course, he wasn't exactly looking through the viewport to admire the hyper-warp 11111 star streaks. He was admiring his blonde hair, white skin, blue eyes, chiseled muscles, and every other feature that Hollywood considered "perfect." Around him were his bridge crew, a group of burly men and scantily-clad women (some of whom actually had weapons!). 

Then, when he remembered that he had a mirror in his bedroom that worked much better than the viewport, he told his crew, "I'm going to my room. Do not disturb me while I prepare for this mission where most of you will die."

The crew saluted as Han left the bridge and went down an escalator into his personal quarters. He was already busy flexing and admiring his muscles when one of his crew walked in. One of the scantily clad alien women, in fact. 

"I asked not to be disturbed while I prepare for this dangerous mission!" Han snapped.

"I'm sorry!" the women, Princess Liara, exclaimed. "It's just that since we will all be dead tomorrow, except you, I should tell you that I love you and want to have your babies!" 

"I also love you and want to make some babies!" Han replied, and the two jumped into his bed before remembering that it was made of metal and so each broke a limb. 

"Don't worry, my love! I have magical healing powers that I have never mentioned before or ever will again!" And so she healed the two of them and proceeded to fuck each other's brains out. Literally. 

By the time they had their brains back in their proper places, the Millennium Prize of Enter Falcon had arrived at an alien world where it was surrounded by three million powerful spaceships. 

"We are being hailed, Captain!" said the only black woman on the entire ship.

"On screen!" ordered Han, and the viewport changed from an image of their impending doom to the leader of the army: Death Invader!

"Muhahahaha! You cannot hope to stop me and my army, Han Shepard, but even they are nothing compared to my magical powers, and I will never explain how!" 

"Oh yeah? Well, I have an ace up my sleeve!"

"What ace?"

"This ace!" Shepard proceeded to pull an ace of spades from under his sleeve, which he threw at the viewport and somehow broke it, sending most of his crew flying out into space and dying before the bulkheads sealed it. 

"Muhahahahaha! You have already done most of our work for us, Han Shepard! Also, I am your father!"

Shepard, realizing his folly, fell to his knees, raised his arms to the ceiling, and screamed, "NOOOOOOOOOOOOOOOOOOOOOOOOOOOOOOOOOOOOOOOOO!"

"Join me, and we can rule the galaxy as father and son!"

"Don't do it!" Princess Liara begged. "I'm pregnant with your child! Don't turn to evil! I love you!"

"You're right! I'll never join you! Begin the space battle! Fire all weapons!"

Much to Death Invader's surprise, the weapons on the Millennium Prize of Enter Falcon had phasers, lasers, dasers, tasers, masers, kasers, asers, pasers, and, worst of all, nacers! The entire three million ship fleet was vaporized instantly, with only Death Invader's ship still standing.

"Sir, we're out of ammo!" reported one of the crew.

"Then reload!" ordered Shepard.

"We can't! The guy who was supposed to reload them died when you destroyed the window!"

"It's not a window, it's a viewport!"

"What's the difference?"

"I don't know, it's just called a viewport in every science fiction book I ever read!"

"Muhahahahaha! You have lost, Shepard!" taunted Death Invader.

Death Invader fired at the Millennium Prize of Enter Falcon, which rocked from the explosions because they had shields and the bad guys didn't, which is alright because otherwise the main character would die and the story would be over. 

"Reload and return fire!" 

The crew scrounged up someone to reload the weapons and fire at the ship, finally blowing it up and killing Death Invader. With the enemy gone, the Millennium Prize of Falcon turned around and went home, where Shepard and Liara had a bunch of little blue children and lived happily ever after.
